soil-chem-098.title: Imogolite, a clay built of nanotubes
soil-chem-098.text: Some clay comes as tubes about 2 nm across. Imogolite, Al2SiO3(OH)4, is an aluminium silicate clay mineral made of a network of these nanotubes. Each tube is 1 nm wide inside, with walls of gibbsite sheets and orthosilicate groups. It was first described in 1962 in Kumamoto prefecture, Japan, and named from imogo, a brownish-yellow soil derived from volcanic ash. It occurs in such soils with allophane, quartz, cristobalite, gibbsite, vermiculite and limonite. Where tephra is basic or the climate dry, allophane and imogolite develop, and {{ref:soil-class-119}} receive the Silandic qualifier.

soil-chem-096.title: Expanded vermiculite in the potting bench
soil-chem-096.text: Once heated and expanded, vermiculite becomes a gardener's material. Mixed with {{ref:soil-class-070}} or composted pine bark, exfoliated vermiculite makes soilless growing media. These speed rooting and hold air, plant food and moisture for release as plants need them. Alone or mixed with soil, it germinates seeds with very little watering. In heavy, sticky soils, mixing in vermiculite up to half the soil's volume creates air channels. In sandy soils it helps the soil hold water and air. Agromineral practice uses vermiculites and zeolites to store moisture in soil, alongside {{ref:soil-fert-072}} for aeration.

soil-chem-111.title: Ferrihydrite, iron oxide as a nanoparticle sponge
soil-chem-111.text: A single gram of ferrihydrite offers several hundred square metres of surface. This widespread, poorly crystalline hydrous iron(III) oxyhydroxide exists only as fine-grained nanoparticles. It forms in soils, waters, aquifers and mining areas, precipitating from oxygenated iron-rich water or through bacterial activity. Its nanoporous particles adsorb arsenic, lead, phosphate and the organic acids met in {{ref:soil-chem-059}} and {{ref:soil-chem-060}}. Ferrihydrite is metastable, a precursor of hematite and goethite, though adsorbed impurities such as silica usually block that change in nature. Under reducing conditions, as in gley soils and often with microbial help, it can turn into green rust, {{ref:soil-chem-109}}. Brief contact with air oxidizes it back to ferrihydrite.

soil-chem-109.title: Fougèrite, the green rust of waterlogged soils
soil-chem-109.text: Fougèrite does not last long in air. This naturally occurring green rust is a layered double hydroxide of ferrous and ferric iron, described only relatively recently. It was first found in forest soils near Fougères, Brittany. The International Mineralogical Association accepted it as a mineral species in 2002. Its brucite-like layers hold Fe2+ and Fe3+, with loosely bound carbonate and water between them. It forms clay-like hexagonal platelets under a micron across. Green rust occurs as fougèrite in {{ref:soil-class-127}}. Exposed to air, it oxidizes, dehydrates and loses carbonate, turning to ferrihydrite and finally to lepidocrocite or goethite.

soil-chem-110.title: Palygorskite, a clay of bristles instead of plates
soil-chem-110.text: Palygorskite grows as bristles rather than plates. Also called attapulgite, it is a fibrous magnesium aluminium clay mineral, (Mg,Al)2Si4O10(OH)·4(H2O). Unlike the layered clays of {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, it has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains linked to magnesium–aluminium octahedral sheets. It forms in shallow lakes, rivers, waterlogged ground and soils, favored by semi-arid conditions and alkaline water rich in magnesium and silica. Its bristle-like crystals do not swell and have a high specific surface area of about 75 to 400 m²/g. It is one type of {{ref:soil-chem-102}}. Farmers use it to carry plant food and to improve water retention and aeration.

soil-chem-089.title: Growing kaolinite from dissolved silica and aluminium
soil-chem-089.text: Kaolinite can crystallize in soil at ordinary temperature and pressure, but only if its ingredients arrive the right way. Silica must come as single molecules in very dilute solution. Aluminium must be six-coordinated with oxygen, as in gibbsite. The reaction is 2Al(OH)3 + 2H4SiO4 → Si2O5·Al2(OH)4 + 5H2O, so five water molecules must be removed for each unit of kaolinite formed. Seasons matter. On basalt in Kivu, kaolinite formed only where wet and dry seasons alternate, not in perennially swampy ground. Wetting–drying cycles also help allophane turn into kaolinite. In soils, disordered amorphous material seems to become ordered kaolinite fairly quickly, without major environmental change.

soil-chem-099.title: Amorphous clays, young minerals not yet in order
soil-chem-099.text: Not every clay has had time to crystallize. Amorphous clays are young mixtures of silica and alumina that have not yet formed regular crystals. They are common in recent volcanic ash deposits such as tephra. Most of their charge comes from hydroxyl groups that gain or lose a hydrogen ion as soil pH changes. That lets them buffer soil pH and attract either cations or anions. High proportions of glass and amorphous colloids, including allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite, define {{ref:soil-class-092}}. Clays without plate-shaped minerals, such as allophanic clays, tend not to show a residual shear strength.

soil-chem-090.title: Halloysite, the kaolinite-group clay that grows as tubes
soil-chem-090.text: Halloysite shares kaolinite's formula, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, but grows as nanotubes. Their walls are 10–15 sheets thick, their outer diameters 50–60 nm and their lengths 0.5–10 μm. This clay of the kaolinite group occurs mainly in recently exposed volcanic soils. It also forms from primary minerals in tropical soils, and glassy basaltic rocks alter to it most readily. Water changes it. Hydrated halloysite has a layer spacing of 1 nm, dehydrated meta-halloysite 0.7 nm. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} rises with hydration, from 5–10 to 40–50 meq/100 g. Allophane alters to halloysite under resilicating conditions. In acidic cave settings at pH 5 or lower, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} alters to its hydrated form, endellite.

soil-chem-085.title: Isomorphous substitution: how clays gain a fixed charge
soil-chem-085.text: A clay's charge is set as the clay forms. While its crystals grow, some cations in the structure are replaced by others of lower valence, carrying less positive charge. This is isomorphous substitution, and it leaves the clay a lasting negative charge. The arithmetic is simple. In the silica sheet, Al3+ may replace Si4+. A site that balanced +4 against −4 now holds +3 against −4, a charge of −1. In the alumina sheet, up to a quarter of the Al3+ may give way to Zn2+, Mg2+ or Fe2+. Mg2+ in place of Al3+ gives +2/−3, again −1. Where the swap happens matters. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} carries its charge mostly in the octahedral sheet, from magnesium replacing aluminium. Beidellite carries it mostly in the tetrahedral sheet, from aluminium replacing silicon. Substitutions in outer layers count for more than inner ones, since charge strength falls off with the square of the distance. Cations in the interlayer must balance the excess negative charge. It attracts water and positively charged ions, some of them useful to plants. Kaolinite has undergone almost no substitution, which is why its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low. This charge does not change with time. That sets it apart from the charge described in {{ref:soil-chem-049}}, which rises as pH rises.

soil-chem-091.title: Smectite, the swelling clay with an open interior
soil-chem-091.text: Smectite clays swell because their layers are not rigidly joined. Smectite is a group of swelling 2:1 clay minerals, chiefly {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, that take water and cations between their layers. The name depends on place: smectite is the usual term in Europe, while North America uses the name of its chief member, and industry calls these clays {{ref:soil-chem-100}}. Each layer is two silica tetrahedral sheets cross-linked through an octahedral sheet of alumina or iron oxide. Isomorphous substitution in both kinds of sheet gives the layers their negative charge. The interlayer between them holds hydrated cations and water. These enter reversibly, so the clay swells as they come in. That open interlayer also gives smectites the highest {{ref:soil-chem-046}} of the clays common in soils; only vermiculite and some zeolites exceed it. Smectites form by weathering of basalt, gabbro and silica-rich volcanic glass, and where hot water or seawater dissolves much of the silica from volcanic ash. Soils with smectite clay expand when wet. Clay soils containing smectite also suffer alkalinity problems more than illite or kaolinite clay soils.

soil-chem-093.title: Montmorillonite, the clay that swells tenfold
soil-chem-093.text: Montmorillonite can swell up to ten times its dry volume. Named after Montmorillon in France, where it was first described in 1847, it is a soft 2:1 clay of the smectite group. An alumina sheet sits between two silica sheets, and its water content varies. Its plate-shaped particles average about 1 μm across and 0.96 nm thick. Resolving one takes about 25,000-fold electron-microscope magnification. Magnesium replacing aluminium in the central sheet leaves nearby oxygens negatively charged and able to attract cations. Its crystals are loosely bound, not bonded face to face. Water enters between them, and the whole surface is open to reactions, which gives it a high {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. It is a characteristic component of swelling soils. It occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions, often mixed with chlorite, muscovite, illite and kaolinite. It is added to drought-prone soils to hold water, and its swelling suits it to drilling mud, earthen dams and levees.

soil-chem-100.title: Bentonite, the swelling clay that seals landfills
soil-chem-100.text: Bentonite can absorb enough water to grow up to eight times in volume. This absorbent swelling clay is made mostly of montmorillonite, in either its sodium or its calcium form. Geologists use the name for a clay rock formed from volcanic ash, usually in seawater, as up to 40–50 wt.% of its silica dissolves away. Sodium bentonite swells far more than calcium bentonite. Adding 5–10% of a soluble sodium salt converts the calcium form to the sodium form. Swelling makes sodium bentonite a self-sealing, low-permeability barrier. It lines landfills, and nearly sodium-saturated clay forms impermeable curtains in soil below dams.

soil-chem-102.title: Fuller's earth, the clay that cleaned wool
soil-chem-102.text: Fuller's earth is named for a trade. Fullers kneaded it with water into woolen cloth to absorb lanolin, oils and other greasy impurities. Today the name covers various clays used as an absorbent, filter or bleaching agent. Products sold as fuller's earth are usually palygorskite, also called attapulgite, or bentonite. Its clays commonly include montmorillonite and kaolinite. In some places the name means calcium bentonite, altered volcanic ash made mostly of montmorillonite. It has a dangerous side. Saturated by heavy rain, it can become thixotropic, so hills, cliffs and slopes that contain it can be unstable.

soil-chem-092.title: Swellers and collapsers: the cations between clay layers
soil-chem-092.text: Whether a clay swells depends on what sits between its layers. In 2:1 clays, the interlayer cations govern how much the clay swells or shrinks as it gains or loses water. Two traits of each cation explain it: how strongly it hydrates, and its hydrated radius. Highly hydrated magnesium ions act as swellers, fully opening vermiculite's interlayer. Poorly hydrated potassium ions act as collapsers, fully closing illite's. In smectites the main interlayer cations are Na+ and Ca2+. Sodium gives the most swelling. With sodium as its main exchangeable cation, montmorillonite can swell to several times its original volume. Calcium smectite swells much less but also shrinks less when dried. Potassium replacing sodium collapses the interlayer, so smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater turns into non-swelling illite. Ammonium is caught the same way. It is fixed mainly between the layers of illite, vermiculite or montmorillonite, with potassium and other ions of similar size and low hydration energy. These cations help set a clay soil's {{ref:soil-phys-028}}.

soil-chem-101.title: Clay that brought worn-out Thai fields back
soil-chem-101.text: In northeast Thailand, farmers restored degraded fields with clay. Bentonite applied to those soils dramatically reversed the degradation and brought higher yields, better crop prices and greater returns. Field trials by the International Water Management Institute and partners in 2002–2003 found that locally sourced bentonite raised yields of rain-fed forage sorghum. Clay-using farmers had higher costs. Their larger, better harvests still let them invest and grow more than farmers who did not use clay. Clays such as calcium bentonite also help water-repellent soils, giving them more surface area per unit volume and supporting aggregation.

soil-chem-086.title: From swelling clays to oxides: the weathering sequence
soil-chem-086.text: A soil's clay records how hard it has been weathered. As weathering and leaching intensify, the dominant clay minerals change: from 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite, through kaolinite, to oxides of iron and aluminium. The starting point depends on the parent material and on the minerals in solution, so source rock and climate both matter. Montmorillonite occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions. Depending on its origin, it may also occur in humid climates. Where rainfall is high, acid soils lose more silica than alumina from their clays, leaving kaolinite. Heavier weathering still produces {{ref:soil-chem-106}}. Rock and chemistry steer the result as well. Acid weathering of feldspar-rich rock in warm climates yields kaolin, alkaline weathering yields illite, and intense weathering of other clay minerals yields gibbsite. Climate gradients show the same pattern. Kaolinite abounds in soils of hot, moist climates. Toward cooler climates illite increases, and toward drier ones smectite. Because clay content tracks climate, the clays of buried ancient soils are used to infer past climates.

soil-chem-106.title: Sesquioxide clays, the last residue of deep weathering
soil-chem-106.text: A sesquioxide clay takes hundreds of thousands of years of leaching to form. These old, highly leached clays are oxides and hydroxides of iron, aluminium and titanium. They remain after heavy rainfall removes most of the silica from alumino-silica clays. They include hematite, iron hydroxide, gibbsite and the manganese mineral birnessite, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils. The name comes from the Latin sesqui, 'one and one-half', for three parts oxygen to two of metal. Not all of them fit that ratio. They are not sticky and do not swell. Soils rich in them, such as lateritic soils, behave much like sand and pass water rapidly. Their {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low, but because their charge varies, they can hold anions as well as cations. They hold large amounts of phosphate, a hold that humified soil organic matter partly blocks. The more goethite they contain, the more phosphorus is locked away from plants. Their dominant iron oxides color these soils from yellow to red.

soil-chem-103.title: Five stages of clay meeting water
soil-chem-103.text: Dry clay packets sit in face-to-face stacks like a deck of playing cards. Clay–water interaction names what happens next, in five stages. First, hydration: the clay absorbs water and swells. In dispersion, water pushes the platelets so far apart that they lose their attraction and spread through the water. Once shearing stops, surface charges draw them back together in flocculation. Deflocculation, or peptization, reverses flocculation. A chemical deflocculant covers the platelets' positive edge charges and greatly weakens their attraction. Finally, in aggregation, ionic or thermal conditions alter the platelets' water layer, strip off the deflocculant and let them stack again.

reviews.clay-minerals-and-colloids: Clay minerals form wherever water weathers rock, and their two kinds of sheet decide much of what follows. Stacked 1:1, as in kaolinite, the layers carry almost no charge and hold few cations. Stacked 2:1, they gain a negative charge from isomorphous substitution, and the cations between the layers set their behavior: potassium locks illite shut, while magnesium and sodium let vermiculite and smectite swell. As weathering and leaching deepen, the dominant clays shift from montmorillonite through kaolinite to sesquioxide clays such as hematite, goethite and gibbsite. Together with organic colloids, these clays hold ions on their charged surfaces and trade them with the soil water.
